title: The Hebrew Feature's Activation Spectrum
takeaway: A histogram of how often feature A/1/416 takes each activation value, with each slice split by an independent Unicode-based score for "is this Hebrew". Strong activations are almost entirely Hebrew, which is the paper's specificity claim for this feature. The blue that survives at strong activations is mostly shared punctuation and whitespace, which the proxy scores as non-Hebrew by construction, so the paper reads it as a fault in the proxy rather than in the feature.
walkthrough:
The article prints no caption here; the sentence quoted alongside is the text that points at the figure, not the authors' own label.

### What you are looking at

This is the specificity picture for the [[hebrew-feature]], written A/1/416 in the paper's [[feature-notation]]. The plot is the paper's standard [[feature-activation-distribution-plot]]: sample a large number of tokens, record what value this one feature takes on each, and build a histogram of those values.

Then colour it. Each token also gets a score from the [[hebrew-script-proxy]], a cheap independent guess at whether the token sits in Hebrew text, computed from Unicode blocks rather than from the model.

### How to read it

The horizontal axis is the feature's activation level, from $0$ to about $9$. Hard zeros are pulled out into their own marker at the far left, because the [[sparse-autoencoder]]'s sparsity penalty leaves most tokens at exactly zero and that spike would otherwise swamp the curve.

The vertical axis is density — how many sampled tokens fall in each activation bin, up to about 20K.

Colour is the proxy score, not the activation. It is the [[log-likelihood-ratio-proxy]] $\log(P(s|\text{Hebrew})/P(s))$, clipped to $\pm 5$: red means the proxy calls the token Hebrew, blue means it does not. Inside the four example panels, the orange highlight is a separate thing — there it marks activation strength.

The strip beneath the main plot renormalises every column to full height, so you read proportions instead of counts.

### What it shows

Two modes. A tall blue mass hugging zero, and a second bump near $7.5$–$8$ that is almost solidly red. Between about $2$ and $6$ there is very little mass at all.

So when this feature fires strongly, the text is Hebrew. That is [[activation-specificity]], and it is the half of the case that matters most, because [[large-activations-dominate]] the feature's effect on the logits.

### The blue at the top

Some blue persists even in the strong-activation bump. That is not counter-evidence. The proxy assigns any string containing a character outside the Hebrew Unicode blocks a probability of $10^{-10}$, so a space, a comma or a digit inside a Hebrew sentence scores deeply negative. The rightmost panel shows exactly that: punctuation and "230,000" embedded in Hebrew. This is the paper's general catalogue of [[proxy-limitations]], and one of its three [[weak-activation-hypotheses]] applied at the other end of the range. The paper hedges — the blue "appears to significantly be" common characters, unquantified.

terms.definition: The plot's title. It means a histogram over sampled tokens of the value one particular feature takes, not a distribution over features.
The identifier of the feature being plotted: model A, dictionary learning run 1, feature index 416 within that run. The paper calls it the Hebrew feature.
How many sampled tokens fall into each activation bin. Labelled in thousands, so 5K is five thousand tokens.
The scalar value the feature takes on a token — the post-ReLU hidden unit of the sparse autoencoder for this dictionary direction.

terms.term: 0 and >0 (the two small markers at the left)
terms.definition: Exactly-zero activations are separated from the merely small ones. Sparsity puts a large point mass at zero, and mixing it into the first bin would distort the curve.
The quantity the colour encodes: how much more likely the token's surrounding string is under the Hebrew hypothesis than under the general text distribution.
Tells you which direction along the colour scale means more Hebrew. Redder is more Hebrew by the proxy's judgment.

terms.term: Blue (negative end of the colour scale)
terms.definition: The proxy judges this token's string as unlikely to be Hebrew. It does not mean the feature is wrong — the proxy has its own failure modes.

terms.term: Red (positive end of the colour scale)
terms.definition: The proxy judges the string as Hebrew: characters drawn from the Hebrew Unicode blocks.

terms.term: White / pale band (middle of the colour scale)
terms.definition: A log-likelihood ratio near zero — the proxy is indifferent, the string is about as likely under Hebrew as under the general distribution.
A cheaply computable score standing in for the human hypothesis about a feature, used as an independent yardstick so the evaluation does not just consult the feature itself.
A contiguous range of Unicode codepoints. Hebrew has its own block, which is what makes a purely mechanical script detector possible here.
Whitespace, punctuation and digits shared across languages. They appear inside Hebrew text but live outside the Hebrew Unicode blocks, so the proxy scores them as non-Hebrew.

terms.term: Conditional distribution strip (the band under the main plot)
terms.definition: The same colour breakdown, renormalised so every activation level fills the full height. It shows the proportion of tokens of each proxy score at that activation, independent of how many tokens there are.

terms.term: Dataset example panels (the four boxes above the plot)
terms.definition: Snippets of real text sampled from activation levels marked by the dotted lines beneath them, so you can see what the feature is responding to at each strength.
Within the example boxes, background shade marks the feature's activation on that token. Darker orange is stronger. This is a different encoding from the blue-red of the histogram.
Connect each example panel to the activation level its snippets were drawn from.
Raw byte tokens shown where a Unicode character was split across several tokens. \xd7 is the first byte of most characters in the basic Hebrew block.
The claim that the feature being on implies the hypothesised context is present. This figure is the evidence for it — read right to left, high activations are red.
The converse claim: that the feature is on whenever Hebrew is present. This figure does not establish it, and the paper reports it as imperfect for this feature.
A separate feature that fires on the \xd7 byte and predicts the bytes completing Hebrew codepoints. The paper offers it as part of why A/1/416's sensitivity looks incomplete.

numbers.meaning: The three parts of the feature's name: model A (one of two one-layer transformers trained with different seeds), dictionary learning run 1, and feature 416 inside that run. Runs differ in dictionary size and L1 coefficient.
The span of activation values this feature actually reaches. Ticks are every 1.0. Nothing beyond about 9 appears because the feature simply never goes higher on the sampled tokens.
Token counts per bin, ticked every 5K. The scale is set by the near-zero spike; everything else is small by comparison.

Almost all sampled tokens sit at or just above zero activation. This is what sparsity looks like: the feature is off for the overwhelming majority of text, and that bulk is deep blue because the overwhelming majority of text is not Hebrew.

numbers.value: ~3.3K (height of the second mode, near activation 7.5–8.0)
numbers.meaning: The strong-activation bump. It is two orders of magnitude smaller in count than the zero spike, but it is where the feature does its work, and it is almost entirely red.

numbers.value: ~2 to ~6 (the flat middle of the x-axis)
numbers.meaning: The trough between the two modes. The feature is rarely partway on; it is mostly either off or firing hard. That gap is what makes the specificity claim clean at the top end.
The log-likelihood ratio is clipped at plus and minus five before colouring. Beyond that the colour saturates, so a very confident non-Hebrew judgment and an extremely confident one look the same.

The probability the script proxy assigns to P(script | s) when the string s contains any character outside the script's Unicode blocks. In log terms that is roughly -23, well past the -5 clip, which is why a single space or comma inside Hebrew text renders as saturated blue.

The approximate activation levels the four example panels are drawn from, marked by the dotted lines. They span the range deliberately: the leftmost panel is Latin, Japanese and Devanagari with no Hebrew at all; the rightmost is dense Hebrew.

numbers.value: 230,000 and 17 (numerals visible in the third and fourth panels)
numbers.meaning: Digits embedded in Hebrew sentences. They are the caveat made concrete — the feature fires on and around them, the proxy scores them as non-Hebrew, and the disagreement is the proxy's fault.

The Pearson correlation between the Hebrew proxy and A/1/416's activations, reported in the surrounding text. It combines specificity and sensitivity into one number, and it is well under 1 mainly because of sensitivity misses, not because of what this figure shows.
The activation correlation of the closest neuron, A/neurons/489. Given elsewhere in the section, it is the reason the paper says no single neuron encodes this.

The byte value that opens the UTF-8 encoding of most basic-block Hebrew characters. It explains why byte tokens litter the example panels and why a second feature exists just to handle the continuation bytes.

numbers.value: ~5 (the threshold the paper uses when talking about the 'upper spectrum')
numbers.meaning: For the analogous Arabic feature the paper quotes specificity of 98% above activation 5, against 25% when barely active. The Hebrew section does not give matching percentages, so the same threshold is being used qualitatively here rather than measured.

numbers.value: 100 million tokens, 10 per context, 4 tokens each side
numbers.meaning: How the visualisation was built: a 100M-token subset of the training data, sampled at ten tokens per context, with a four-token window shown around each displayed token. This is why the example snippets are short and disconnected.
